actions.investigated_summary: The account named chenwei in system 1 (app1.log) performed both USDT transfers: 30,000 USDT at 2024-03-01 09:15:03 and 12,000 USDT at 2024-03-02 22:43:55, both to destination TBait8888Wallet, totalling 42,000 USDT. Each transfer sits within a chenwei LOGIN/LOGOUT session from external IPs 203.0.113.77 and 198.51.100.23. No other account performed a transfer; liuyu has only a single DOWNLOAD event. The same-named accounts across the two systems CANNOT be treated as the same person on this evidence: README.txt states the systems share no account database, no shared account ID / authentication token / device-session correlation / Windows logon artifact exists, and the IP profiles differ (public in app1.log vs RFC1918 in app2.log). Non-equivalence is a limitation of the evidence, not a positive finding of two distinct individuals.
limitations: Attribution is bounded to the account namespace of system 1 (app1.log); extending it to the finance-department employee chenwei or to the chenwei of system 2 is unsupported.
The 'no shared account database' premise rests solely on README.txt (case-description context), not on a technical artifact.
Absence of a linking artifact is not proof of two different people; it only means equivalence is unestablished.
No Windows-native evidence exists (no event logs, registry, prefetch, Amcache), so logon/execution corroboration could not be applied.
Both logs share an identical filesystem mtime (1790556630) with empty md5, indicating export/copy rather than in-place capture; provenance and line completeness are unverified.
The user= field is self-attributed; no cryptographic or session-level proof of the true actor is available.
Destination TBait8888Wallet is uncorroborated by any ledger, blockchain or counterparty evidence.

actions.capability_basis: Two plaintext log exports plus README case description; no Windows-native identity artifacts available.
actions.limitation: Identity assessment is bounded: within system 1 the transfers are attributed to the chenwei account, but cross-system identity equivalence between app1.log chenwei and app2.log chenwei is unestablished. No authentication record, account database export, device correlation or Windows logon artifact is available. The README's 'no shared account database' premise is contextual, not technically verified. Non-equivalence is a limitation of the evidence, not a positive finding of separate individuals.

actions.capability_basis: app1.log plaintext export containing all recorded TRANSFER events.
actions.limitation: Transfer activity is fully enumerated within the available log scope: two transfers totalling 42,000 USDT to TBait8888Wallet, both under the chenwei account in system 1, each within a chenwei LOGIN/LOGOUT session. No transfer is attributed to any other account. However, the log lines are self-attributed (user= field) with no independent session or cryptographic proof, and the destination wallet TBait8888Wallet has no corroborating ledger or blockchain evidence. Log provenance is unverified (identical filesystem mtime, empty md5).

actions.text: The chenwei account in app1.log (system 1, external IPs 203.0.113.77 and 198.51.100.23, performed the 42,000 USDT transfers) and the chenwei account in app2.log (system 2, RFC1918 IPs 10.20.0.5 and 10.20.0.9) are the same individual, and therefore a single identity timeline can be constructed across both log sets.

actions.attempted_resolution: Not resolvable with the available evidence. Resolution requires authentication records (password hashes, SSO/AD membership, MFA device IDs, session tokens), an account database export from both systems (employee IDs, emails, creation dates), and/or device-level correlation artifacts (machine GUIDs, hardware IDs, browser fingerprints, proxy/VPN logs). Until such evidence is obtained, the safe position is: transfers are attributable only to the chenwei account in system 1; cross-system identity equivalence is an open question, not an established fact.
actions.impact: Any downstream conclusion that merges the two log sets into a single chenwei identity timeline — or that attributes the 42,000 USDT transfers to the finance-department employee chenwei — is unsupported and must be retracted or re-scoped to the system-1 account namespace only.
actions.limitation: The README's framing of chenwei as a finance-department employee is case-description context, not a technical artifact, and cannot be used to bridge the two systems.

raw_model_proposal_v2.integration_summary: Specialist result D1 answers Q1 within the evidence ceiling: the USDT transfers (30,000 + 12,000 = 42,000 USDT to TBait8888Wallet) are attributable only to the account named chenwei in system 1 (app1.log). Cross-system identity equivalence between the chenwei of app1.log and the chenwei of app2.log is NOT supported — the two systems share no account database per README.txt, no linking artifact exists, and the IP profiles (public vs RFC1918) cannot discriminate. Q1 is closed as answered with the explicit disposition 'supported' for the attribution half and the negative half documented as a limitation, not as a positive finding. COV1 (identity-assessment) and COV2 (transfer-activity) are marked partial/covered respectively, with the coverage limits recorded. A hypothesis capturing the unsupported same-person inference is created and marked weakened so downstream consumers cannot silently promote it. A material contradiction is recorded between the README's 'same chenwei, finance dept' framing and the technical evidence's inability to establish cross-system equivalence. Evidence relevance is set: E3 and E4 are high_value (primary logs), E2 is relevant (contextual, unverified), E1 is irrelevant (filesystem metadata only, mtime = export time).
limitations: Username strings are non-unique identifiers; no account ID, email, employee ID or authentication artifact links the chenwei entries of app1.log to those of app2.log.
The claim that the two systems share no account database rests solely on README.txt (case-description context), not on a technical artifact such as an exported account database.

Absence of a linking artifact does not prove two different people; it only means the evidence does not establish equivalence. Non-equivalence is a limitation of the evidence, not a positive finding of separate individuals.

No Windows-native evidence exists (no event logs, registry, prefetch, Amcache), so execution and logon corroboration rules cannot be applied and the transfer attribution cannot be independently validated beyond the app1.log user field.

Both logs were created at an identical timestamp (1790556630) with empty md5 values, indicating export/copy rather than in-place capture; provenance, completeness and integrity of the log lines are unverified.
Log lines are self-attributed (user= field); there is no cryptographic or session-level proof that the recorded user field reflects the true actor, and no evidence of log tampering analysis.
The destination identifier TBait8888Wallet is uncorroborated; no ledger, blockchain or counterparty evidence is available.
Task metadata exposes no platform scenario and no registered source scopes, so the requested 'windows' scope could not be validated against a registered capability.
warnings: Identity-trap risk: the same username 'chenwei' appears in both log files, which invites the natural but unsupported inference that one person performed all activity. The evidence explicitly does not support this.

Attribution ceiling: the transfers are supportable only as 'the account named chenwei in system 1'. Extending that to the finance-department employee chenwei or to the chenwei of system 2 is an unsupported leap.

Do not merge the two log sets into a single identity timeline; the IP address profiles (public 203.0.113.x / 198.51.100.x vs RFC1918 10.20.0.x) are mutually consistent with either two systems or two accounts and cannot discriminate.
The evidence base is extremely small (three plaintext files, 978 bytes total); any conclusion beyond the literal log lines is inference.
Log provenance is unverified: both logs share an identical filesystem mtime (1790556630) with empty md5, indicating export/copy rather than in-place capture; lines may be truncated.

result_semantic_payload.summary: All USDT transfers recorded in the seized device's logs are attributed to the account name "chenwei": 30,000 USDT on 2024-03-01 09:15:03 and 12,000 USDT on 2024-03-02 22:43:55, both to destination TBait8888Wallet (app1.log). No USDT transfer appears under any other account; the only other account, liuyu, has a single DOWNLOAD event. The evidence does NOT support treating the "chenwei" name in app1.log and the "chenwei" name in app2.log as the same person. The README states the two systems are unrelated internal systems that share no account database, so the name is a non-unique, uncorroborated identifier. The two logs are also mutually inconsistent as one identity: app1.log shows chenwei logging in from external IPs (203.0.113.77, 198.51.100.23) while app2.log shows chenwei from RFC1918 internal IPs (10.20.0.5, 10.20.0.9), and the README places chenwei in the finance department on an office workstation. No cross-system linking artifact (no shared account ID, no authentication token, no device/session correlation, no Windows logon/execution evidence) exists in the evidence set. Conclusion: chenwei is the strongest-supported attribution for the transfers within system 1 only; cross-system identity equivalence is an unsupported inference that must not be asserted.

The two log sources are exports from two unrelated internal systems that share no account database, so the username field is not a shared or unique identity key across systems.

No evidence in the available set links the chenwei entries of app1.log to the chenwei entries of app2.log: there is no shared account identifier, authentication credential, device/session correlation, or Windows logon/execution artifact; the only common attribute is the string 'chenwei'.

limitations: IP-address class alone is not an identity discriminator; a single person may legitimately log in from both internal and external networks.
